chunks: "I'd start from two equations: V equals IR plus K e omega and T equals K tI .
From the first, the current is (V minus K e omega) over R and from the second the torque is proportional to current.
Substituting gives torque falling linearly with speed: T equals K t over R (V minus K e omega) . So the torque-versus-RPM curve is a straight line.
On the torque axis it starts at stall torque, K tV over R , with the shaft held still: that's the maximum torque, with the maximum current V over R .
It falls to zero torque at the no-load speed, about V over K e — a bit under, because of friction.
The slope is the speed regulation, R over (K eK t) : a small R makes a stiff motor whose speed barely drops with load.
Current versus torque is also a straight line through the origin, I equals T over K t , plus a small offset for friction.
Current versus speed falls linearly from stall current to almost zero at no-load speed.
Back-EMF versus speed is a line from zero up to nearly V , and versus torque it falls from nearly V to zero. The IR drop is whatever is left.
The implications: peak mechanical power is at half the stall torque and half the no-load speed, but peak efficiency is much closer to no-load speed, at low current.
So you size a motor to run at maybe 10 to 30% of stall torque, and never sit at stall, because there it's all heat.
Changing the supply voltage slides the line parallel to itself, which is how PWM sets speed."
